headings.title: Installation records, process ownership and bounded removal

html:
Installation records, process ownership and bounded removal

Compiled installation maintenance uses a registry of selected instances, separate resource inventories and OS process observations. These records let it distinguish an owned application generation from another instance's shared runtime, a replaced path or a later customer addition. They do not make an uninstall transactional or turn a PID or file path into permanent proof of ownership.

This page explains the record store, process owner, privilege helper and Windows finalizer. The lifecycle orchestrator selects instances, checks shared references, confirms plans and controls services. Compiled dependency generations cover the earlier setup/publication workflow; build instructions remain the command reference.

Registry and resource inventories

The store uses <compiled-data-root>/.lifecycle. key accepts only server or gateway and a 1–64 character instance name beginning with a lowercase letter or digit, with lowercase letters, digits, underscores and hyphens thereafter. selected returns sorted keys from both installations and retained data; selecting all roles takes the union. Shared-resource protection is calculated by the caller, not by this key-selection helper.

Record Role
registry.json Schema-v1 dictionaries for installations, resources and retained data.
manifests/<resource-id>.json Original resource path/category/root identity and individual entries.
operation.lock, gate.lock, leases/*.lock Cross-process lifecycle coordination chosen by callers.
processes/<role>.<instance>.json Application, supervisor and process-group observations plus resource references.
removal.json Maintenance progress, completion or pending Windows executable removal.

load does not create storage when the registry is absent. Existing records must pass path checks, schema/section validation and, on POSIX, current-user ownership and private mode checks. Malformed or unsupported records fail instead of becoming an empty registry. save requires a private directory and replaces one JSON file; callers own locking and valid registry contents.

allowed_resource accepts paths strictly below the category root for applications, runtimes, environments, launchers, browsers, tools, downloads, managed data or installation receipts. It rejects the category root itself and unknown categories. check_path rejects parent traversal and existing symlink/reparse components; consumers can permit a final link when operating on the link itself. These are path-boundary checks, not evidence that a user approved removal.

sequenceDiagram participant Owner as Lifecycle owner participant Store as Resource store participant Files as Filesystem participant Records as Manifest / registry files Owner->>Store: Track selected resource path and category Store->>Files: Check category boundary and root identity alt Same path ID and root identity already recorded Store-->>Owner: Reuse original inventory ID else New resource identity Store->>Files: Inventory names, kinds, identities and file sizes opt Application, runtime or launcher Store->>Files: Hash recorded regular files end Store->>Records: Replace separate resource manifest Store-->>Owner: Update caller registry in memory and return ID Owner->>Records: Save registry under caller lock end Note over Owner,Records: Manifest publication and registry publication are separate writes Owner->>Store: Remove an approved, unreferenced resource manifest Store->>Files: Check root and every recorded entry before mutation loop Entries in reverse inventory order Store->>Files: Recheck identity and anchor existing POSIX entries alt Recorded entry already missing Store->>Store: Continue resumable removal else Directory contains later additions Store->>Store: Retain directory and record its path else Recorded entry still matches Store->>Files: Unlink file/link or remove empty directory end end Store-->>Owner: Retained directories or propagated failure opt Manifest removal returned successfully Owner->>Records: Save completed resource progress end

A resource ID is derived from its path; its manifest also records device/inode identity. When that root identity still matches, track deliberately reuses the original inventory rather than claiming files added later. A fresh inventory records links as leaves, rejects special file types and walks directories in sorted order. It is a live traversal, not an atomic snapshot.

Application/runtime/launcher manifests include file hashes, but validate_entry and removal compare identities rather than hashes. Editing a recorded file in place does not exempt it from removal. A replacement inode causes refusal; later unrecorded files keep their containing directories nonempty and therefore retained. Recorded links are unlinked without deleting their external targets. Missing entries are tolerated so an interrupted operation can retry.

All entries are checked before the first deletion, then checked again during removal. POSIX uses no-follow directory descriptors to keep ancestor operations anchored and checks the root identity when encountered. Windows uses path checks and identity comparisons. These checks do not freeze a concurrently changing filesystem. A later failure can leave earlier deletions completed; there is no rollback of the whole manifest.

Lifecycle locks use shared/exclusive flock on POSIX and byte-zero file locking on Windows. Lock files must be regular, private and single-link. Acquisition polls nonblocking every 50 ms until a monotonic deadline; long maintenance waits can emit one progress message. Scope exit releases the lock while retaining its reusable file. The dependency installer uses a separate lock described in the setup guide.

Process observations and graceful stop

A running marker records the application process, native supervisor, process group, installation key and resource IDs. running checks for an existing live instance and publishes its marker under the operation lock, then releases that lock while the application runs. On scope exit it removes only a marker still matching its own recorded value. It deliberately avoids reacquiring the operation lock, which maintenance may hold while waiting for shutdown.

sequenceDiagram participant App as Compiled application participant Runtime as Process owner participant OS as Operating system participant Marker as Instance marker participant Maintenance as Maintenance caller App->>Runtime: Enter running-instance scope Runtime->>Marker: Under operation lock, reject matching live instance Runtime->>OS: Observe application, supervisor and group identities Runtime->>Marker: Publish observations and resource references Runtime-->>App: Release lock and run application Note over App,Marker: On application exit, remove only its still-matching marker Maintenance->>Runtime: Request graceful stop Runtime->>Marker: Read selected application identity Runtime->>OS: Compare fresh application identity alt Marker absent or application identity differs Runtime-->>Maintenance: Return without signaling else Matching application Runtime->>OS: Revalidate supervisor and Windows group if applicable alt Ownership changed Runtime-->>Maintenance: Refuse and request manual stop else Identity still matches Runtime->>OS: SIGTERM supervisor or send Windows CTRL_BREAK Runtime->>OS: Poll original supervisor identity until gone or deadline alt Supervisor identity gone Runtime->>Marker: Remove marker Runtime-->>Maintenance: Stop observation complete else Timeout or signaling failure Runtime-->>Maintenance: Raise and retain installation files end end end

Linux identity includes PID, process start ticks and executable path; zombies are absent. Windows uses process creation time and image path. Other platforms use ps start/command output. Handled lookup errors also return no identity, so this is an observation rather than a complete health or ownership proof. Malformed marker data can still raise.

stop first validates the application marker, then separately validates the supervisor. Windows also checks the recorded process group and uses a disposable Python helper to attach to its console and send CTRL_BREAK. POSIX sends SIGTERM to the supervisor. The wait checks disappearance/change of the original supervisor identity; it does not independently enumerate every descendant process. There is no forced-kill escalation after the default thirty-second timeout. Identity checks reduce PID-reuse mistakes but are not an atomic OS signal handle.

default_environment constructs Server state/identity/TLS paths or Gateway instance/TLS/job/browser/artifact/lease paths without creating them. apply supplies only missing process environment values, then changes working directory. Explicit current environment values survive; a failed directory change does not roll back the preceding environment assignments.

Permission fallback and backup reads

flowchart TD Caller[Caller-selected manifest and operation] --> Local[Try ordinary removal, inventory or backup] Local --> Result{Outcome} Result -->|Success| Return[Return result] Result -->|Other error| Fail[Propagate error] Result -->|PermissionError| Terminal{Interactive call without terminal?} Terminal -->|Yes| Refuse[Refuse elevation] Terminal -->|No| Plan[Write private temporary plan with roots and identities] Plan --> Platform{Platform / interaction policy} Platform -->|POSIX| Sudo[Run isolated helper through sudo or sudo -n] Platform -->|Interactive Windows| UAC[Request UAC and wait for helper] Platform -->|Unattended Windows| Refuse[Refuse elevation] Sudo --> Helper[Recheck boundaries and execute bounded operation] UAC --> Helper Helper --> JSON[Write structured result or error] JSON --> Check{Usable successful result?} Check -->|No| Fail Check -->|Yes| Backup{Backup result?} Backup -->|Yes| Copy[Copy through exclusive private archive writer] Backup -->|No| Return Copy --> Return

The local removal attempt may already have deleted earlier entries before a PermissionError. Elevated retry uses the same manifest and missing-entry rules; it is not a retry of an untouched filesystem. Other errors do not trigger elevation. The caller's approved resource scope is carried in a private temporary plan along with its data/cache roots and invoking account information.

Interactive maintenance without a terminal is refused. POSIX unattended mode uses sudo -n and succeeds only when OS policy permits it without prompting. Windows unattended elevation is refused; interactive UAC waits for the helper handle. The helper runs isolated Python with a fixed bootstrap, then uses the same store checks. A nonzero command result without result JSON fails; structured helper errors also fail. Temporary plan/result files are removed on scope exit.

For backup, the orchestrator requires stopped instances, managed data identity and a destination outside source data. It inventories regular files and uses open_recorded_file to check the final open descriptor. POSIX walks no-follow ancestor descriptors and verifies the recorded root when encountered; this prevents ancestor redirection without freezing file contents against concurrent writes. The archive includes file hashes and restore metadata, and the caller reopens it to verify stored contents. Links are not copied as ordinary backup files.

A permission fallback asks the helper to create a verified temporary archive with further elevation disabled, transfers ownership/access to the invoking account and copies it through the exclusive private archive writer. That writer never opens an existing destination for replacement and removes only its own incomplete file after failure. Backup failure prevents the orchestrator from proceeding to purge. Separate external data paths remain the operator's backup responsibility.

Windows executable removal after exit

An executing Windows launcher can keep its own file open. The orchestrator defers that launcher manifest when the running executable lies within it, completes other selected work and records pending-executable-removal.

sequenceDiagram participant Owner as Uninstall owner participant Temp as Temporary maintenance runtime participant Parent as Invoking native launcher participant Helper as Detached Windows finalizer participant Store as Registry and removal journal Owner->>Temp: Write deferred plan with parent PID, roots and selected manifests Owner->>Helper: Spawn isolated detached process outside current job Owner->>Store: Record pending executable removal Owner-->>Parent: Return from maintenance Helper->>Parent: Open parent handle and wait when available Parent->>Parent: Exit and release executable handle Helper->>Store: Acquire operation and gate locks loop Deferred manifests Helper->>Helper: Remove recorded entries without interactive elevation Helper->>Store: Remove completed resource ID and save registry end alt All deferred removals succeed Helper->>Store: Write complete and retained paths else Removal fails Helper->>Store: Write pending status with cleanup recovery instruction end Helper->>Temp: Spawn PowerShell cleanup waiting for helper exit Helper->>Helper: Exit Temp->>Temp: PowerShell removes only temporary maintenance directory

Scheduling success means a helper was started, not that removal finished. The plan stores a parent PID; the finalizer waits on the handle if it can open that process, otherwise it proceeds. This uses a different mechanism from the application marker's creation-time comparison. A spawn failure removes the deferred plan and propagates.

The finalizer saves registry progress after each completed manifest. If removal raises, it records a retryable journal with instructions to rerun --cleanup from the original download. It can return zero after recording that pending result, so exit status alone is insufficient: inspect removal.json. Plan-read/setup errors before its removal handler can fail without that journal update. Failure to launch the final PowerShell cleanup can leave temporary files even after resource removal. That last cleanup receives only the temporary maintenance path, not arbitrary installed-resource paths.

Review and validation limits

The lifecycle caller's selected registration, removal-plan, backup and removal paths were inspected to connect these helpers to real operations. Its complete service, legacy adoption and install/update protocols remain separate review areas. Current isolated lifecycle cases cover shared references, retained data, untracked additions, replaced resources, symlink leaves, verified backups, interrupted removal and stale PID observations. They use temporary installations and mocked dependency setup; this documentation work does not uninstall a real instance, request elevation or exercise live Windows UAC.
